recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say why the ordinary power rule and the ordinary exponential rule both fail, and what you do instead.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Take logarithms on both sides
steps.margin_note: First mark. Say why the two familiar rules do not apply before taking logarithms — that sentence is the method the examiner is looking for, and it is what separates this from an ordinary power.
steps.memory_tip: A variable base and a variable exponent at the same time means you should take logarithms. Logarithms turn the power into a product.
lines: The base x and the exponent x are both variables.
needs a constant exponent, and the exponential rule
Neither one applies, so take logarithms first.
(take log of both sides of y = xˣ; y > 0 because x > 0)
(log(pᵐ) = m log p, with p = x and m = x)

recall.must_convey: That neither the power rule nor the exponential rule applies because base and exponent are both variable, so logarithms are taken, giving log y = x log x.
accept: base and power are both x so neither standard rule works
take log on both sides to get log y equals x log x

steps.why: Taking logarithms turns the power into a product, and a product is something the product rule can handle. That is why the method is called logarithmic differentiation.
common_mistakes: Writing the derivative as x · xˣ⁻¹ by using the power rule with a variable exponent.
Writing the derivative as xˣ log x by using the exponential rule with a variable base.

steps.label: Differentiate and put y back
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Multiply back by y and then replace y with xˣ — the answer must be written in x alone. Check at x = 1: xˣ = 1 and 1 + log 1 = 1, so the derivative is 1.
steps.memory_tip: The left side always gives one over y times dy/dx, so y always has to be multiplied back at the end.
lines: Differentiate both sides with respect to x.
The left side needs the chain rule,
the right side the product rule.

recall.must_convey: That differentiating gives (1/y)(dy/dx) = 1 + log x, so dy/dx = xˣ(1 + log x).

steps.why: Differentiating log y gives (1/y)(dy/dx), so y has to be put back before the answer is complete. Stopping at 1 + log x is a common way this mark is lost.
common_mistakes: Stopping at (1/y)(dy/dx) = 1 + log x without multiplying by y.
Differentiating x log x as log x only, losing the 1 that comes from x · (1/x).
lines_compact: Differentiate both sides with respect to x.
The left side needs the chain rule,
the right side the product rule.

insider_note: Base and exponent are BOTH variable, so neither the power rule nor the exponential rule applies — take logarithms first. The left side then needs the chain rule and the right the product rule.
